articles.title: Alpha-beta oscillatory dynamics underlying auditory inhibitory control in children
articles.content: Response inhibition, the ability to withhold an unwanted response, is a fundamental component of cognitive control. While evoked responses in inhibitory tasks have been widely studied, induced oscillatory dynamics, particularly in the auditory modality and in children, remain largely unexplored. Here, we used magnetoencephalography (MEG) to examine induced alpha (8-12 Hz) and beta (13-20 Hz) oscillations during passive listening and an auditory Go/Nogo task in 67 children (6-14 years) and 16 adults (20-30 years). During passive listening, both groups showed an early alpha power increase in right fronto-temporo-parietal regions, followed by an alpha decrease in temporal regions. Under inhibitory demands, adults displayed a late alpha and beta power increase within a left fronto-temporo-occipital network, whereas children exhibited an early-onset, prolonged beta power decrease in somatomotor and temporo-parietal regions. Our findings indicate that children and adults engage spectrally, temporally, and spatially different neural dynamics during inhibitory control: in children, oscillatory modulation emerges earlier and is dominated by a beta decrease in sensorimotor regions, whereas adults recruit synchronized late alpha-beta dynamics in executive networks, possibly reflecting more efficient and evaluative inhibitory processing.
articles.author: Finnilä, E., van Bijnen, S., Kujala, J., Parviainen, T.

articles.title: How striatal neurons influence decision-making depends on broader circuit context: evidence from theory-driven cell type identification
articles.content: Neural cell types are often conceived as having fixed computational roles, yet their behavioral contributions may depend on the broader circuit state. In the striatum, for example, direct and indirect pathway spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are typically described as facilitating or suppressing actions, respectively. However, emerging observations of striatal activity, such as modulation related to action timing, action vigor, and reactive inhibition, call this dichotomy into question. Here we develop a state-space framework linking striatal population activity to decision dynamics by combining a spiking cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBGT) model with large-scale in vivo recordings from mice performing a two-choice task. Modeled activity patterns guided the inference of putative striatal SPN subtypes in the empirical recordings, enabling reconstruction of decision trajectories through an underlying state space. Across simulated and experimental data, these trajectories revealed a shared set of decision dynamics and identified three state-dependent roles of indirect pathway activity: preserving uncertainty when active alone, signifying choice commitment when coactive with the direct pathway in the same action channel, and slowing decisions when recruited in the opposing channel. To interpret these roles mechanistically, we mapped state transitions onto previously described basal ganglia control ensembles (responsiveness, pliancy, and choice) that translate circuit activity into the evidence accumulation process, and we found that each role was associated with a distinct pattern of control ensemble engagement that tunes decision policy. These analyses support a context-dependent view of SPN function, in which their moment-to-moment impact emerges from the evolving profile of dynamics throughout the CBGT circuit.
articles.author: Yu, Z., Verstynen, T., Rubin, J.

articles.title: Postpartum resource scarcity reshapes maternal care, offspring prioritization, and the steroid-sensitive medial preoptic area
articles.content: Parental care requires balancing offspring needs with environmental constraints, yet how resource scarcity alters the organization of maternal responses remains poorly understood. Here, we examined maternal behavior, offspring prioritization, and steroid receptor-associated extracellular matrix organization in postpartum rats exposed to limited bedding and nesting (LBN) or control conditions with ample nesting materials. LBN increased pup-directed and reduced self-directed behaviors but also increased behavioral entropy, a measure of behavioral fragmentation, indicating less predictable caregiving sequences. LBN dams preferentially retrieved male pups first, whereas control dams preferentially retrieved females first. LBN also increased the proportion of pup-investigation time directed toward males compared with controls. In offspring on postnatal day 10, corticosterone was elevated in female but not male LBN pups, a pattern that paralleled the maternal male bias. To identify associated neurobiological changes, we assessed steroid receptors and extracellular matrix organization in the medial preoptic area (mPOA), a key region for maternal behavior. LBN increased numbers of estrogen receptor  (ER)- and androgen receptor (AR)-immunoreactive cells, reduced perineuronal net (PNN) abundance, and decreased receptor-positive cell enwrapment. Because PNNs constrain structural plasticity, these findings suggest that the postpartum environment alters the organization of steroid receptor-associated extracellular matrix, potentially modulating experience-dependent plasticity in neurosteroid-sensitive circuits. In sum, LBN increases the levels of maternal engagement while reshaping its temporal organization and allocation, accompanied by selective remodeling of steroid-sensitive preoptic architecture. Therefore, maternal adaptation to adversity may be better understood as changes in caregiving allocation strategies rather than a simple gain or loss of maternal care.
articles.author: Aspesi, D., Soriano, V., Rolle, S., Mahrous, M. Y., Brenhouse, H., Krishnan, K., Bangasser, D. A.

articles.title: Sentence-level neural dynamics in speech motor cortex
articles.content: Prior recordings from speech motor cortex have revealed phonemic, syllabic, articulatory and speech-sequence representations, while more recent studies indicate that activity may also reflect higher-order features of speech production. However, whether speech motor cortex is sensitive to the linguistic organization of sentences remains unclear. Here we show that single-unit activity in speech motor cortex contains information about sentence-level linguistic structure. In three BrainGate2 participants with implanted microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, we recorded neural activity during an instructed-delay speech task comprising English sentences, word lists, syntactically structured nonword sentences and nonword lists. Neural activity in areas 6v and 55b contained speech- and language-related components, with stronger stimulus-condition effects in 55b, and stimulus condition was decodable in all three participants. In two larger datasets, semantic categories of English sentences were decodable from neural activity. These findings demonstrate that speech motor cortex encodes information about linguistic structure and semantic content at the level of sentences.

articles.title: The Computational Grammar of Human Behaviour in a Biological Environment
articles.content: Human behaviour unfolds as an extended stream of spontaneous actions shaped by environmental demands and the agent's goals. The organisation of these actions, situated between setting abstract goals and concrete movement execution, remains poorly characterised. Here, we introduce DynaClade, an unsupervised temporal action segmentation algorithm for human full-body motion capture data, and apply it to freely moving participants navigating ecologically realistic risky foraging environments in virtual reality. DynaClade identifies discrete actions whose kinematic characteristics and spatial distributions correspond to environmental affordances, supporting the validity of the approach. Among these actions, we discovered a hitherto undescribed movement pattern defined by increased body sway without locomotion. Action sequences were highly non-random and showed clear history dependence beyond first-order Markov structure, most of which was explained by a second-order prediction. This higher-order structure was well captured in a hidden Markov model, in which some of the observed actions were associated with more than one latent state. Each of these latent states corresponded to the same action in a distinct action context. These findings suggest that spontaneous human actions are predominantly selected based on the current action and context, rather than following pre-planned or habitually assembled sequences.
articles.author: Serratos Hernandez, U. D., Goekay, U., Kornemann, L., Hutabarat, Y., Sen, D., Bach, D. R.

articles.title: Loss of GluN2A Selectively Impairs Excitatory Synaptic Integration in Hippocampal Somatostatin Interneurons
articles.content: N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) are widely considered key determinants of excitatory synaptic kinetics and activity-dependent plasticity, yet their specific contribution to postsynaptic potentials across distinct hippocampal CA1 cell types remains poorly defined. Null variants in GRIN2A are strongly associated with epilepsy-aphasia spectrum disorders, and GluN2A loss has recently been linked to delayed electrophysiological maturation of parvalbumin interneurons, a process regulated by somatostatin interneuron activity. Here, we used Grin2a haploinsufficient and knockout rats to determine how GluN2A depletion affects excitatory synaptic transmission, integration and firing across CA1 pyramidal neurons, parvalbumin interneurons and somatostatin interneurons. Using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in acute hippocampal slices, we found that NMDARs made no discernible contribution to shaping Schaffer collateral-evoked EPSP kinetics, temporal summation or spike recruitment in CA1 pyramidal neurons at physiological resting potentials. Hebbian long-term potentiation at pyramidal neuron Schaffer collateral synapses was also preserved. Parvalbumin interneuron EPSP kinetics and synaptically evoked firing were similarly unaffected. By contrast, GluN2A loss selectively prolonged EPSP decay in CA1 somatostatin interneurons, increasing EPSP area, enhancing frequency-dependent temporal summation and elevating action potential output during repetitive and theta-frequency synaptic stimulation. These changes occurred alongside an increase in intrinsic excitability, indicating a cell-type-specific alteration by GluN2A loss. Selective enhancement of somatostatin interneuron recruitment provides a candidate mechanism - upstream of delayed parvalbumin interneuron maturation - and may contribute to hippocampal network dysfunction in GRIN2A-related disorders.
articles.author: Hunter, D. W., Kaese, H., Kind, P. C., Wyllie, D. J.

articles.title: Same Movements, Different Skills: How Context Shapes Learning in Humans and Neural Networks
articles.content: What determines whether experiences are integrated into shared representations or split? Motor skill learning offers a revealing test: when two tasks require an identical sequence of movements, both intuition and theory suggest that practice in one should generalize to the other. Yet we find that changing context can make identical movements different skills. In simple recurrent networks trained on the same sequence across contexts, splitting was greatest when strong contextual inputs coincided with a high initial weight scale; neither alone sufficed. Greater representational separation coincided with separate context-specific learning curves. Humans practicing the same finger sequence while alternating between two performance-irrelevant contexts likewise exhibited context-specific curves, rather than the single continuous trajectory observed when practicing in a single context. State-space modeling favored split learning states in humans and very weakly coupled states in the most context-dependent networks. These findings have broader implications for understanding how learning generalizes across contexts.

When neuroscience meets machine learning: a taxonomic scoping review of machine and statistical learning approaches in sub-Saharan Africa
articles.content: In high-resource economies, computational neuroscience research frequently employs machine learning (ML) and statistical learning (SL) techniques. While these methods provide effective ways to analyse multimodal, high-dimensional, and complex data they are underexplored in low resource settings. This taxonomic scoping review uses a systematic methodological approach to synthesise the application of ML and SL techniques in neuroscience research in sub-Saharan Africa. In addition to discussing findings, strengths, limitations, and future prospects, the work classifies current research by neuroscience domains, applications, learning tasks, datasets, tools, and techniques. In order for African researchers to contribute to and benefit from the global computational neuroscience landscape, our review contends that low- and middle-income countries must create and augment context-specific and representative datasets and incorporate appropriate features for model training. Future studies should focus on pragmatic rather than complex modelling, external validation, reproducibility, interpretability, and utilise real-world data to determine clinical utility.
articles.author: Deshendran Moodley

articles.title: Validation of the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised in patients with disorders of consciousness
articles.content: ObjectiveOur objective was to validate the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R).DesignWe conducted a multicenter study across neurology, intensive care, neuro-rehabilitation, and nursing departments in Hungary. Thirty-one patients (17 males; mean age 49.1 ± 16.1 years) with disorders of consciousness (DOC) following severe acquired brain injury were assessed. Two independent raters reassessed the same patients within a one-week window to evaluate inter-rater and intra-rater reliability. We assessed reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa and evaluated concurrent validity using Spearman’s rank correlation.ResultsConcurrent validity with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was strong across all raters and time points (rho = 0.882–0.934, p < 0.001). Inter-rater reliability for the total score was excellent at initial assessment (wk = 0.977) and remained high at follow-up (wk = 0.977). Diagnostic classification agreement between raters was nearly perfect (wk = 0.936–1.000).ConclusionThe Hungarian CRS-R is a valid and reliable instrument that preserves the robustness of the original version. Its implementation fills a critical gap in national healthcare by providing an evidence-based tool to reduce DOC misdiagnosis rates.
articles.author: András Attila Horváth

articles.title: Coordination without command: active inference and the route to embodied intelligence
articles.content: Embodied intelligence depends on bodies whose contact with the environment, distribution of load and capacity for action are only partly known and are changed by movement. We argue that this creates a practical reason to organize inference through distributed, hierarchical and plural processes, using active inference to relate local belief updating, contextual constraints and action selection within a common framework. The proposal brings together established ideas from factorized inference, distributed control and embodied robotics, distinguishing their mathematical description from the location of computation and authority over action. The octopus provides biological motivation through its combination of peripheral sensorimotor processing and central influences on behavior, while an articulated hexapod illustrates selected architectural choices through six leg-local predictive controllers coupled by neighbor messages and a shared mechanical body. The simulation includes intact locomotion and movement following programmed limb withdrawal and graph reconfiguration, although these observations do not isolate the contribution of inference or establish remapping. Together, the biological example and computational illustration clarify how local inferential processes may remain coordinated across bodily interfaces and timescales without a controller prescribing the complete joint trajectory.
articles.author: Alexander D. Shaw

articles.title: Case Report: Clinical applications of extended-duration remote ambulatory EEG monitoring: lessons from real-world cases
articles.content: BackgroundTraditional ambulatory electroencephalography (EEG) and inpatient epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) admissions face significant operational limitations including: short recording windows (typically 24–72 h), high costs, technician shortages, and physical restrictions on daily activities.MethodsThis article presents clinical utility frameworks and three illustrative real-world case studies utilizing the REMI Remote EEG Monitoring System—a wireless, wearable 4-sensor electrode-setup (10-channel EEG montage system) montage system integrated with cloud data transmission and post-acquisition artificial intelligence (AI) electrographic seizure detection algorithms.ResultsIn Case 1, a 39-year-old female with suspected recurrent epilepsy experienced three focal seizures after the standard 72-h monitoring window, allowing initiation of targeted antiseizure therapy. In Case 2, extended monitoring in a 57-year-old male with long-standing epilepsy experiencing new exercise-induced symptoms ruled out electrographic seizures, avoiding unnecessary medication escalation. In Case 3, a 52-year-old male with worsening episodic déjà vu exhibited focal interictal rhythmic activity, providing objective data to guide shared decision-making and successful initiation of antiseizure treatment.ConclusionExtended-duration remote EEG monitoring bridges key diagnostic gaps by offering flexible, real-world data collection over extended timeframes (up to 30 days). This approach optimizes clinical triage, clarifies event etiology, and improves ambulatory epilepsy care without overburdening tertiary health care infrastructure.
articles.author: Timothy Ryan

articles.title: What shared responses reveal about audience behavior: neural prediction and the emerging potential of peripheral synchrony
articles.content: Predicting audience responses to dynamic media remains a significant challenge in neuromarketing and neuroforecasting. Intersubject correlation (ISC) has been proposed to address this need by quantifying the temporal similarity of neural, physiological, and behavioral responses among individuals exposed to the same stimulus. This narrative mini-review examines how ISC relates to preferences, judgments, and behavior and proposes a conceptual framework for interpreting its predictive value. Across modalities, ISC consistently reflects shared stimulus processing and is associated with attention, alongside additional links to engagement, memory, and higher-order narrative processing. Neural ISC has shown associations with individual, group, and population-level outcomes, although findings vary by neural modality, analytic approach, and behavioral endpoint. Peripheral ISC derived from gaze, heart rate, electrodermal activity, and facial expressions provides complementary information about interindividual alignment, but direct evidence for predicting consumer outcomes remains limited. At the same time, neural and peripheral measures capture various aspects of shared response dynamics, and combining them in a multimodal ISC approach may help distinguish synchronization in different functional domains, including perceptual, attentional, autonomic, affective, and valuation-related processes, and clarify their relationship to the target outcome. The proposed framework therefore conceptualizes ISC as a probabilistic predictor whose predictive value depends on which functional processes underlie the observed synchrony and their relevance to the specific outcome of interest.

articles.title: Human cortical high-gamma power scales with movement rate in healthy participants and stroke survivors
articles.content: Motor cortical high-gamma oscillations (60-90 Hz) occur at movement onset and are spatially focused over the contralateral primary motor cortex.
